title: Best SMS & WhatsApp Marketing Tools for Ecommerce & D2C Brands in 2026
summary: 8 voice AI agent platforms compared on telephony ownership, latency, compliance, pricing, and channel coverage. Honest reviews with limitations
body_markdown:
Email open rates keep sliding. SMS and WhatsApp haven't: both still see open rates north of 90%, and that gap is why most D2C brands now treat them as core revenue channels, not add-ons.


But picking a tool isn't as simple as "text people more." Deliverability, list compliance, WhatsApp template approval, and Meta's per-conversation fees all sit between a subscription and actual revenue. The platform matters more than most brands expect going in.


This guide compares 8 SMS and WhatsApp marketing platforms for ecommerce, looking at deliverability, automation depth, WhatsApp commerce features, and real all-in pricing.


## What Actually Matters When Choosing an SMS/WhatsApp Marketing Tool


Most platforms look the same in a demo: send a text, watch it convert. The differences show up once you're running real campaigns at real volume. Here's what's worth checking before you commit.


1.


Deliverability and compliance: Carrier filtering and 10DLC registration in the US, WhatsApp template approval through Meta, and basic list hygiene all affect whether your messages actually land. A platform that handles registration and compliance for you saves real headaches later.


2.


Segmentation and automation depth: Cart abandonment, back-in-stock alerts, post-purchase flows, win-back campaigns. Look at how easily you can build these without needing a developer every time you want to adjust a trigger.


3.


WhatsApp commerce features: Not every SMS tool does WhatsApp well. Check for native catalog support, buttons and quick replies, and whether WhatsApp and SMS share the same customer profile or live in separate silos.


4.


Ecommerce platform integrations: Shopify, WooCommerce, and your helpdesk should sync cleanly: order data, customer tags, and purchase history need to flow into your segments automatically.


5.


Two-way conversations, not just broadcasts: Some tools are built for one-way blasts. Others support real conversations, replies, and even text-to-buy. That distinction matters more for WhatsApp than SMS.


6.


Reporting tied to revenue: Open rates are a weak signal. Look for revenue-per-send, attribution by flow, and conversion tracking that ties messages to actual orders, not just clicks.


7.


The real cost per message: The subscription price rarely includes carrier fees, Meta's per-conversation charges on WhatsApp, or overage costs once you scale past your plan's included volume. Model the cost at your actual send volume, not the advertised starting price.

## 1. Plivo


Best for: Ecommerce brands that want SMS and WhatsApp on one platform, with no markup on messaging costs and voice available on the same infrastructure if they need it later.


Plivo runs its own carrier network across 190+ countries rather than reselling someone else's, which shows up most clearly in pricing: SMS and WhatsApp are billed at cost, with no platform markup layered on top of Meta's or the carrier's rate. For a D2C brand running cart-abandonment texts and WhatsApp order updates side by side, that means one dashboard, one API, and one bill covering both channels instead of stitching together an SMS tool and a separate WhatsApp BSP.


Segmentation and automation flows (cart recovery, back-in-stock, post-purchase) run through Plivo's no-code studio or its API, so ops teams can build and adjust campaigns without waiting on engineering, while developers still have full API access for custom logic tied into Shopify, HubSpot, Salesforce, or Zendesk.


### Key features


-


SMS and WhatsApp on one platform with shared customer context; a conversation that starts as a text and continues on WhatsApp doesn't lose history


-


No markup on WhatsApp conversations; you pay Meta's published rate directly


-


No-code studio for building campaigns and flows, plus full API/SDKs for custom integrations


-


Owned carrier infrastructure across 150+ countries, useful for brands selling internationally


-


Voice available on the same platform if WISMO or order-confirmation calls become part of the mix later


### Limitations


-


Less purpose-built for ecommerce marketing specifically than tools like Klaviyo or Postscript, which come with deeper pre-built segmentation and revenue-attribution reporting out of the box.


-


No native loyalty or reviews features; brands wanting SMS bundled with loyalty (like Yotpo) would need a separate tool for that piece.


-


Smaller ecosystem of pre-built ecommerce marketing templates compared to platforms built specifically for the DTC marketing use case.


### Pricing


Pay as you go. SMS and WhatsApp are billed at cost, with no platform markup and no quarterly minimums.


## 2. Twilio


Best for: Enterprise brands already running other communications (voice, email, verification) on Twilio who want to add SMS and WhatsApp marketing without introducing a new vendor.


Twilio owns its own telephony and messaging infrastructure and has the broadest connector catalog of any platform in this list, which matters if your marketing stack already pulls from Twilio for other things. For SMS and WhatsApp specifically, you're working with Twilio's Programmable Messaging APIs rather than a purpose-built marketing dashboard, so segmentation, flows, and campaign building are things you assemble yourself or through a third-party layer on top.


### Key features


-


Owned telephony and messaging infrastructure with strong global reach


-


Programmable SMS and WhatsApp APIs, plus Studio for building basic messaging flows visually


-


Largest connector and integration catalog in the space


-


Strong compliance posture (SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR)


### Limitations


-


No purpose-built ecommerce marketing layer. Segmentation, campaign automation, and revenue attribution require building on top of the API or bringing in a separate marketing tool.


-


SMS and WhatsApp are separate products with separate billing; they don't share customer context without additional integration work (Segment or custom development).


-


More engineering-heavy than the marketing-first platforms in this list. Not a fit for a team without developer support.


### Pricing


Pay as you go. SMS and WhatsApp are billed separately, at Twilio's published per-message and per-conversation rates.


## 3. Klaviyo


Best for: Email-first D2C brands that want to add SMS as a natural extension of a marketing program they're already running, without adopting a separate SMS-only tool.


Klaviyo is built around email first, with SMS as an add-on rather than a parallel core product. If your marketing team already lives inside Klaviyo for flows, segmentation, and email campaigns, adding SMS keeps everything (customer profiles, purchase history, flow triggers) in one place rather than syncing data between two platforms. The trade-off is that SMS pricing runs on a separate credit system layered on top of your email plan, and WhatsApp isn't natively built in the way SMS is.


### Key features


-


Unified customer profiles across email and SMS, with shared segmentation and flow triggers


-


Deep pre-built ecommerce automations: abandoned cart, browse abandonment, post-purchase, win-back


-


Strong analytics and predictive segmentation across both channels


-


350+ platform integrations


### Limitations


-


SMS is billed through a separate credit system on top of the email plan cost, so the real price is two numbers added together, not one.


-


WhatsApp isn't a native channel; brands wanting WhatsApp typically need a separate integration or tool alongside Klaviyo.


-


Pricing is based on active profiles, so cost climbs with list size regardless of how much you actually message, making list hygiene a real cost lever.


-


SMS credits don't roll over month to month.


### Pricing


Email plans start at $20/month for 251–500 active profiles and scale up by tier. SMS is billed separately through a monthly credit system, with 150 credits included on paid plans and additional credits priced per message.


## 4. Attentive


Best for: High-volume, high-revenue ecommerce brands that want a managed, high-touch SMS program with dedicated support, rather than a self-serve tool they configure themselves.


Attentive positions itself at the enterprise end of SMS marketing: quote-based pricing, quarterly minimums, and a managed relationship rather than a self-serve signup. That model makes sense once SMS is a meaningful, proven revenue channel and the quarterly commitment is small relative to what the channel already generates. Below that point, the minimums are a real cost most brands can't justify.


### Key features


-


Managed onboarding and dedicated support, positioned for brands with established SMS programs


-


Deliverability and compliance handling built for high-volume senders


-


AI-assisted campaign and flow tools


-


Deep segmentation for large, complex subscriber lists


### Limitations


-


Pricing isn't published; brands get a custom quote, typically with quarterly minimums in the thousands of dollars.


-


Minimums make it a poor fit for brands under roughly $1M in annual revenue, where the commitment outweighs what SMS is actually driving yet.


-


No WhatsApp; SMS and email are the core channels.


-


The managed, sales-led model means less self-serve flexibility than Postscript or Klaviyo for brands that want to configure things themselves.


### Pricing


Custom quotes. Entry point is roughly $300/month plus about $0.01/SMS, with typical spend landing in the $1,500–$5,000+/month range once quarterly minimums are factored in. No published self-serve pricing.


## 5. Postscript


Best for: Shopify-native D2C brands that want transparent, self-serve SMS pricing without enterprise minimums or a sales call.


Postscript is built specifically for Shopify and publishes its pricing openly, which stands out in a category where most enterprise-tier competitors quote custom. It bills SMS at cost with no markup on the carrier fee, and its lower tiers have no quarterly commitment, making it a realistic starting point for brands still proving out SMS as a channel rather than ones already running it at scale.


### Key features


-


Shopify-native automations: cart abandonment, browse abandonment, welcome flows, upsells


-


Transparent, published per-SMS pricing with no markup on carrier fees


-


No quarterly minimums on entry-level plans


-


Strong benchmarking data published from its own merchant base


### Limitations


-


Shopify-exclusive; not a fit for brands on WooCommerce, Magento, or other platforms.


-


SMS only. No WhatsApp, and email is not a core part of the platform.


-


Less enterprise-grade deliverability infrastructure than Attentive at very high volume.


### Pricing


Starter is $0/month with a $49/month minimum spend. Growth is $100/month. Professional is $500/month. Per-SMS rates run $0.007–$0.015 depending on tier, plus roughly $0.004 in carrier fees.


## 6. Yotpo SMSBump


Best for: Brands already using Yotpo for reviews and loyalty who want SMS bundled into the same platform instead of adding a separate SMS-only tool.


Yotpo SMSBump's real advantage shows up for brands that already have Yotpo running for reviews or loyalty: SMS sits in the same dashboard, pulling from the same customer data, rather than syncing reviews, loyalty points, and messaging across three separate tools. For a brand starting from scratch on SMS with no existing Yotpo footprint, the case is weaker, since the pricing bundles across products in a way that's harder to isolate and compare against a dedicated SMS tool.


### Key features


-


SMS integrated with Yotpo's reviews and loyalty data, so campaigns can reference review requests or loyalty tier directly


-


No-code campaign and flow builder


-


Free tier available for brands testing SMS at low volume


-


Shared customer profile across SMS, email, reviews, and loyalty


### Limitations


-


Pricing is bundled and modular across Yotpo's product suite, which makes it harder to isolate the true cost of SMS alone compared to a dedicated tool.


-


No WhatsApp support.


-


The strongest case for this tool depends on already using (or wanting) Yotpo's reviews and loyalty products; as a standalone SMS tool it doesn't clearly beat Postscript or Attentive.


### Pricing


Free tier available. Paid plans start around $89/month, with bundled and modular pricing that scales by order volume.


## 7. Gupshup


Best for: High-volume brands in India and Southeast Asia that need SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS handled through a single enterprise-grade vendor.


Gupshup is the infrastructure layer of choice for a lot of large Indian and APAC brands, processing messaging volume most Western SMS/WhatsApp tools never touch. Its strength is regional: deep carrier relationships across India and APAC, bank-grade security, and a single dashboard covering SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS together. For a Western D2C brand without a meaningful India/APAC presence, that regional depth doesn't translate into an advantage worth the added complexity.


### Key features


-


SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS in one platform with a unified dashboard


-


Strong carrier relationships and delivery rates across India and Southeast Asia


-


Enterprise-grade security and audit-grade message logs, used by regulated verticals (banking, fintech)


-


Handles very high message volume reliably


### Limitations


-


Pricing isn't transparent; every quote is custom, and reviewers consistently flag this as a friction point.


-


Adds a markup on top of Meta's WhatsApp rate, on top of the platform fee.


-


Overkill for a typical Western D2C brand without India/APAC volume; the regional strengths don't offset the added cost and complexity elsewhere.


-


Dashboard reporting is reported as slower than competitors, per user reviews.


### Pricing


Custom, volume-based pricing. WhatsApp carries roughly a $0.001/message markup on top of Meta's published per-message rate.


## 8. WATI


Best for: SMBs and smaller D2C brands that want a no-code WhatsApp team inbox and broadcast tool without building on the raw API themselves.


WATI wraps the WhatsApp Business API in a shared team inbox, broadcast tools, and a no-code flow builder, which makes it accessible to a small team without a developer. It's WhatsApp-only, so it's not a fit for a brand that wants SMS and WhatsApp under one roof, but for a brand whose customers live on WhatsApp specifically, it's a lower-lift way to get a team inbox and basic automation running.


### Key features


-


Shared team inbox for WhatsApp conversations across multiple agents


-


No-code broadcast and flow builder


-


Pre-built automation templates for common use cases


-


Onboarding support aimed at non-technical teams


### Limitations


-


WhatsApp only. No SMS or email, so brands need a separate tool for other channels.


-


Pricing is in USD, which some users report makes billing inconsistent month to month for teams paying in other currencies.


-


BSP markup on top of Meta's rate isn't officially disclosed, making true cost harder to pin down than platforms that publish it.


-


Positioned by some reviewers as feeling dated next to newer, faster-moving WhatsApp-first tools.


### Pricing


Plans run $49–$299/month, plus Meta's per-message rate with an estimated (not officially disclosed) BSP markup of around 20%.


## Choosing the Right SMS/WhatsApp Marketing Platform


The right pick depends less on which platform has the most features and more on what's already true about your stack: which channels you actually need, how much volume you're sending, and whether you want a marketing-first tool or straightforward messaging infrastructure you build on top of.


Brands that want SMS and WhatsApp handled on one platform without a per-message markup are best served by Plivo, especially if voice ever enters the picture (WISMO calls, order confirmations) since it sits on the same infrastructure. Twilio makes sense in a similar way, but mainly for enterprise teams already running other communications on it; outside of that, its lack of a purpose-built marketing layer is a real gap compared to the rest of this list.


For brands already deep in an email program, Klaviyo is the more natural home for SMS: profiles, segments, and flow triggers stay unified rather than synced across tools, though the separate SMS credit system and lack of native WhatsApp are worth planning around. Yotpo SMSBump follows a similar logic for brands already running reviews or loyalty through Yotpo, where bundling SMS into the same customer data outweighs the harder-to-isolate pricing.


Volume and revenue stage decide the Postscript-versus-Attentive question more than features do. Postscript's transparent, no-markup pricing and lack of quarterly minimums make it the more realistic starting point for a Shopify brand still proving SMS out. Attentive's quarterly minimums only pencil out once SMS is already a meaningful, proven revenue line, at which point the managed support and deliverability infrastructure start to earn their cost.


Gupshup and WATI both serve narrower, more regional or channel-specific needs: Gupshup for brands with real India or APAC volume that want SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS under one enterprise vendor, and WATI for smaller teams whose customers live specifically on WhatsApp and want a no-code inbox without touching the raw API.


## The Bottom Line


There's no single best tool here, because "best" depends on which channel actually matters to your customers and how much of your stack you want unified versus specialized. What's consistent across every platform in this list is that the advertised rate is rarely the real one: carrier fees, Meta's conversation charges, and BSP markups all sit between the pricing page and the invoice. Model your actual send volume against the full cost, not the headline number, before committing to any of them.


That said, if the deciding factor for you is fewer vendors and fewer surprise line items, Plivo is worth shortlisting first: SMS and WhatsApp at cost with no markup, on the same platform, with voice sitting right there if you ever need it. It won't out-feature Klaviyo on segmentation or Attentive on managed support, but for a brand that just wants messaging infrastructure it can trust the invoice on, it's the cleanest starting point on this list.

## Frequently Asked Questions


#### Which is better for ecommerce: SMS or WhatsApp?


Depends on where your customers already are. SMS works everywhere with no app required, which makes it the safer default for US-heavy brands. WhatsApp wins on engagement in markets where it's the default messaging app (India, Latin America, parts of Europe) and supports richer formats like catalogs and buttons. Most established brands eventually run both.


#### Do I need a separate tool for SMS and WhatsApp, or can one platform handle both?


A few platforms handle both natively. Plivo and Twilio cover SMS and WhatsApp on one platform with a shared API. Klaviyo added WhatsApp via its Mobile plan but it's still secondary to SMS. Postscript, Attentive, and WATI are single-channel by design.


#### What's the real cost per message, not the advertised rate?


Almost always higher than the headline number. Carrier fees, Meta's per-message WhatsApp rate, and BSP markups (commonly 12–20% on platforms like Interakt or WATI) stack on top of the platform fee. Plivo and Postscript are the two in this list that publish pricing with no markup added.


#### Is there a minimum revenue or list size before SMS/WhatsApp marketing makes sense?


For SMS generally, no. For Attentive specifically, yes: quarterly minimums make it hard to justify below roughly $1M in annual revenue. Postscript, Klaviyo, and Plivo have no such floor.


#### Which platform is easiest to set up without a developer?


Postscript, Klaviyo, WATI, and Yotpo SMSBump are all no-code and built for marketing teams to run directly. Plivo and Twilio also offer no-code builders but lean more toward teams that may want API access later.


#### Can I migrate from one platform to another later without losing my subscriber list and flows?


Subscriber lists (opted-in numbers) generally transfer. Flows and automations don't; you rebuild them on the new platform. This is the real switching cost, more than the subscriber list itself, so it's worth weighing before committing to a platform with steep lock-in like Attentive's managed contracts.


#### Do I need WhatsApp Business API approval before I can send marketing messages?


Yes. Every platform that offers WhatsApp (Plivo, Twilio, Gupshup, WATI) requires Meta's template approval process before you can send outbound marketing messages. Approval timelines vary, budget a few days before your first campaign, not same-day.
